## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Objective

This notebook compares how LR, Cox, RF and RSF attribute predictive importance across the same ULB predictors. The Methodology Notebook (Section 9) explains RSF through permutation importance, SHAP and LIME, but provides no comparable view for the other three models. Here, all four are fitted on identical subsamples and their importance rankings are compared directly.

### 1.2. Motivation

Supervisor review (October 2026) asked how the RSF explanations compare with LR, RF and Cox. Since the four models produce different kinds of importance (standardised coefficients for LR and Cox, permutation importance for the forests), the comparison is made on rankings rather than raw magnitudes.

## 2. Libraries and Data

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
## Step 1: Load required packages (dplyr loaded last to avoid select() masking)
library(survival)
library(randomForestSRC)
library(glmnet)
library(caret)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(pander)
library(dplyr)
```

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
## Step 1: Set seed - same position as Methodology Notebook Section 3.1, so the
## downsampled working dataset below reproduces fraud_subset exactly
set.seed(44940076)

## Step 2: Load data
fraud_data <- read.csv("creditcard.csv", header = TRUE)
fraud_data <- na.omit(fraud_data)

## Step 3: Survival variables (Methodology Notebook Section 5.1)
fraud_data$time   <- 1:nrow(fraud_data)   # proxy time index
fraud_data$status <- fraud_data$Class      # event indicator

## Step 4: Downsampled working dataset (Methodology Notebook Section 5.2)
fraud_cases     <- subset(fraud_data, Class == 1)
nonfraud_cases  <- subset(fraud_data, Class == 0)
nonfraud_sample <- nonfraud_cases[sample(nrow(nonfraud_cases), 50000), ]
fraud_subset    <- rbind(fraud_cases, nonfraud_sample)

dim(fraud_subset)
```

## 3. Design

Each of 30 repeated stratified 70-30 splits draws an importance subsample from the training partition, keeping all fraud cases and 10,000 non-fraud cases, as in the Methodology Notebook (Section 9.2). Predictors are standardised within each subsample so that LR and Cox coefficient magnitudes are comparable across predictors. All four models use the primary predictor set (V1-V28, Amount and raw `Time`):

* **LR:** absolute standardised coefficients
* **Cox (ridge):** absolute standardised coefficients at the cross-validated penalty
* **RF and RSF:** permutation importance (`importance = "random"`, 50 trees, as in Section 9.2)

```{r explain-ulb, eval=!file.exists("explain_ulb.rds")}
## Step 1: Predictor set and storage
pred_set  <- c(paste0("V", 1:28), "Amount", "Time")
n_splits  <- 30
imp_rows  <- vector("list", n_splits)
coef_rows <- vector("list", n_splits)

## Step 2: Set seed
set.seed(44940076)

## Step 3: Fit all four models on each split's importance subsample
for (i in 1:n_splits) {
  message("Explainability split ", i, " of ", n_splits, " - ", Sys.time())

  # 1. Stratified split, then importance subsample from the training partition
  idx     <- createDataPartition(fraud_subset$status, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
  train_i <- fraud_subset[idx, ]
  fr      <- train_i[train_i$status == 1, ]
  nf      <- train_i[train_i$status == 0, ]
  sub     <- rbind(fr, nf[sample(nrow(nf), 10000), ])

  # 2. Standardise predictors within the subsample
  sub_s <- data.frame(scale(sub[, pred_set]),
                      status = sub$status,
                      time   = sub$time,
                      Class  = factor(sub$Class, levels = c(0, 1)))

  # 3. LR
  lr_fit  <- glm(reformulate(pred_set, response = "status"),
                 data = sub_s, family = binomial)
  lr_coef <- coef(lr_fit)[pred_set]

  # 4. Cox (ridge)
  cox_cv   <- cv.glmnet(as.matrix(sub_s[, pred_set]), Surv(sub_s$time, sub_s$status),
                        family = "cox", alpha = 0)
  cox_coef <- as.matrix(coef(cox_cv, s = "lambda.min"))[pred_set, 1]

  # 5. RF (classification), permutation importance
  rf_fit <- rfsrc(reformulate(pred_set, response = "Class"), data = sub_s,
                  ntree = 50, nodesize = 15, splitrule = "gini",
                  nthread = 4, fast = TRUE, importance = "random")
  rf_imp <- rf_fit$importance[pred_set, "all"]

  # 6. RSF, permutation importance
  rsf_fit <- rfsrc(as.formula(paste("Surv(time, status) ~", paste(pred_set, collapse = " + "))),
                   data = sub_s, ntree = 50, nodesize = 15, splitrule = "logrank",
                   nthread = 4, fast = TRUE, importance = "random")
  rsf_imp <- rsf_fit$importance[pred_set]

  # 7. Store
  imp_rows[[i]]  <- data.frame(split = i, feature = pred_set,
                               LR = abs(lr_coef), Cox = abs(cox_coef),
                               RF = rf_imp, RSF = rsf_imp)
  coef_rows[[i]] <- data.frame(split = i, feature = pred_set,
                               LR = lr_coef, Cox = cox_coef)
}

## Step 4: Save
saveRDS(list(imp  = do.call(rbind, imp_rows),
             coef = do.call(rbind, coef_rows)), "explain_ulb.rds")
```

## 4. Results

### 4.1. Importance Rankings by Model

```{r explain-ulb-ranks}
## Step 1: Load results and average importance across splits
explain_ulb <- readRDS("explain_ulb.rds")
model_cols  <- c("LR", "Cox", "RF", "RSF")

imp_mean <- explain_ulb$imp %>%
  dplyr::group_by(feature) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(model_cols), mean), .groups = "drop")

## Step 2: Rank each predictor within each model (1 = most important)
rank_tab <- imp_mean %>%
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(model_cols), ~ rank(-.x), .names = "{.col}_rank")) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(RSF_rank)

pander(rank_tab %>% dplyr::select(feature, dplyr::ends_with("_rank")),
       caption = "Importance Rank by Model (1 = Most Important, 30 Splits)")

## Step 3: Top five predictors per model
top5 <- sapply(model_cols, function(m) imp_mean$feature[order(-imp_mean[[m]])][1:5])
pander(data.frame(Rank = 1:5, top5), caption = "Top Five Predictors by Model")

## Step 4: Rank of raw Time in each model, for inline reporting
time_ranks <- rank_tab %>% dplyr::filter(feature == "Time") %>%
  dplyr::select(dplyr::ends_with("_rank"))
```

### 4.2. Agreement Between Models

```{r explain-ulb-agreement}
## Step 1: Spearman rank correlation between models' importance profiles
rank_cor <- cor(imp_mean[, model_cols], method = "spearman")
pander(round(rank_cor, 3), caption = "Spearman Rank Agreement Between Models")

## Step 2: Top-five overlap between each pair of models
top5_overlap <- outer(model_cols, model_cols, Vectorize(function(a, b)
  length(intersect(top5[, a], top5[, b]))))
dimnames(top5_overlap) <- list(model_cols, model_cols)
pander(top5_overlap, caption = "Number of Shared Top-Five Predictors")

## Step 3: Rank heatmap
rank_long <- rank_tab %>%
  dplyr::select(feature, dplyr::ends_with("_rank")) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-feature, names_to = "model", values_to = "rank") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(model   = factor(sub("_rank", "", model), levels = model_cols),
                feature = factor(feature, levels = rev(rank_tab$feature)))

ggplot(rank_long, aes(x = model, y = feature, fill = rank)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = rank), size = 2.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "steelblue", high = "white") +
  labs(title = "Importance Rank by Model (ULB, Ordered by RSF)",
       x = "Model", y = "Predictor", fill = "Rank") +
  theme_bw()
```

### 4.3. Direction of Effects (LR and Cox)

```{r explain-ulb-direction}
## Step 1: Mean signed standardised coefficients with 95% split intervals.
## Positive = higher fraud odds (LR) or higher fraud hazard (Cox).
dir_tab <- explain_ulb$coef %>%
  dplyr::group_by(feature) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    LR_mean  = mean(LR),  LR_lo  = quantile(LR, 0.025),  LR_hi  = quantile(LR, 0.975),
    Cox_mean = mean(Cox), Cox_lo = quantile(Cox, 0.025), Cox_hi = quantile(Cox, 0.975),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Same_direction = sign(LR_mean) == sign(Cox_mean)) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(abs(LR_mean)))

pander(dir_tab, digits = 3, split.table = Inf,
       caption = "Standardised Coefficients: LR vs Cox (Mean and 95% Split Interval)")

## Step 2: Share of predictors where LR and Cox agree on direction
pct_same_direction <- mean(dir_tab$Same_direction) * 100
pct_same_direction
```

**Observations:** `V14` is the one predictor all four models rank highly (first or second for LR, RF and RSF, and third for Cox), and `V4` ranks in the top six for all four. Beyond these, the models divide by the outcome they model rather than by model family: LR and RF agree closely (Spearman 0.873, with four shared top-five predictors), RSF agrees moderately with both (0.604 and 0.552), and Cox shows almost no agreement with any other model (-0.002 to 0.187). Raw `Time` illustrates the divide. It ranks first for Cox and third for RSF, but 20th for LR and 23rd for RF, so it matters only to the two models whose survival response it duplicates, consistent with the Time Sensitivity Analysis.

LR and Cox agree on the direction of only `r round(pct_same_direction, 1)`% of the coefficients, close to chance, although most disagreements involve small coefficients whose intervals span zero, and the strongest shared predictors (`V14`, `V10`, `V4`, `V11`) agree. The LR coefficient magnitudes should also be read with caution: `glm` reported fitted probabilities of 0 or 1 in 28 of the 30 splits, a sign of quasi-separation, and the very wide LR intervals (for example `V17`, -33.5 to 0.01) show that a few splits inflate the mean magnitudes. Cox's ridge coefficients are shrunk and dominated by `Time` (-1.10), which accounts for much of its disagreement with the other models.

## 5. Synthesis

The four models agree on the strongest ULB fraud signal, `V14` and to a lesser extent `V4`, but beyond that their explanations depend on the outcome being modelled. The two classification models agree closely, while the two survival models diverge from them, largely because they weight raw `Time` heavily as a duplicate of their own response. Explanations of RSF on ULB should therefore be read as explanations of a survival model that partly encodes the proxy time ordering, rather than as a model-independent account of what drives fraud.
